summary: This informational RFC accompanies the text/markdown registration. It gives background on the design philosophies behind Markdown, discusses strategies for storing it locally, and registers additional Markdown syntax variants.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the extra explanation for Markdown's official label. It tells the story of why Markdown looks as it does and lists its different flavors.

questions: which markdown flavor should i use
subtitle: Why Markdown was designed to be forgiving, and how to preserve variant information when Markdown moves between systems

tldr.problem: Markdown exists as multiple variants tailored to different communities, and when Markdown content moves to storage systems like files or databases, the variant and other metadata must be preserved somehow.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC explains Markdown's design philosophy of informality and human-friendliness, provides strategies for storing variant information in different systems (filenames, extended attributes, adjacent files), and registers specific Markdown variants like MultiMarkdown, GitHub-Flavored, Pandoc, and CommonMark.
tldr.outcome: Markdown communities have documented, canonical variants registered with IANA, and standard techniques for preserving metadata when Markdown is stored offline.

facts.label: Registered variants
facts.value: 8 (Original, MultiMarkdown, GFM, Pandoc, Fountain, CommonMark, kramdown-rfc2629, Markdown Extra)

today: RFC 7764 is an Informational RFC published in March 2016. It remains the definitive companion to RFC 7763 on Markdown registration and guidance. The Markdown variant registry it establishes continues to operate, with both the eight variants defined in the RFC and additional community-contributed variants registered since publication.

sections.title: Text on a Spectrum
sections.content: Text can be stored and processed along a spectrum of techniques. Plain text contains only character codes with no formatting information. At the other extreme, binary data uses specialized bit patterns that software must interpret. Between them lies formatted text, which uses ordinary characters overloaded with special meanings—like using `<` to start an HTML tag instead of the less-than sign. Formal markup languages like XML follow strict rules and require skill to use. Lightweight markup languages like Markdown use simple syntax designed for humans to enter with basic text editors, without needing to learn complex rules. Markdown is an informal plain-text formatting syntax intentionally targeted at non-technical users.
sections.plainLanguage: Text can be plain (just letters), formatted (with symbols that mean things), or binary (computer code). Markdown is a friendly type of formatted text that is easy for anyone to use without special training.

sections.title: Why Markdown Is Forgiving
sections.content: Markdown's informality is a deliberate design choice. John Gruber created Markdown after bad experiences with strict XML and XHTML, which can break entire websites if one site publishes invalid XHTML that gets copied across feeds. Markdown rejects the notion of validity: there is no such thing as invalid Markdown. Instead of rejecting malformed input, Markdown processors should try to make sense of what they receive—a principle inspired by Postel's Law from networking. If Markdown output is not what the author wants, the author should experiment with changes or switch tools, not conform to rigid rules. Since its creation in 2004, Markdown has become an Internet meme, with different communities adapting it for screenplays, scholarship, mathematics, and more, each building on the common core while adding their own extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Markdown was made to be friendly and forgiving because strict rules kept breaking things. If something looks close to Markdown, the processor tries to understand it. This lets different communities use Markdown for their own purposes without fighting the rules.

sections.title: How to Save Markdown Metadata
sections.content: Internet media types work best for content in protocols like HTTP and email, where metadata can be sent in headers. But when Markdown moves to files, databases, or content management systems, the variant parameter and other metadata must be preserved using the systems available. This RFC describes strategies: record the variant in the filename (e.g., `readme.pandoc.markdown`), store metadata in a separate adjacent file with a related name, prepend MIME headers to the Markdown content as if it were an email message, generate a batch script with processing instructions, process the Markdown to its target format in advance, or rely on context (directories, naming conventions). For version control systems like Git and Subversion, named properties and extended file attributes can store the metadata. Each strategy trades off simplicity against precision and reversibility.
sections.plainLanguage: When you save Markdown to a file, you can put the variant name in the filename, save the variant in a separate file, add it to file properties, or other creative methods. This keeps computers aware of which flavor of Markdown is being used.

sections.title: Registered Markdown Variants
sections.content: The RFC registers eight Markdown variants to provide canonical identifiers that communities and tools can rely on. Original is John Gruber's original Markdown syntax. MultiMarkdown (MMD) is a superset adding tables, footnotes, and citations. GitHub-Flavored Markdown (GFM) adds strikethrough, fenced code blocks, tables, and syntax highlighting, with HTML sanitization built in. Pandoc is a general-purpose converter designed for multiple output formats beyond HTML, supporting definition lists, mathematics, and more. Fountain is a specialized variant for screenplays. CommonMark is a standard, unambiguous specification with comprehensive tests, longer than Original and drawing more from Unicode, UTF-8, and HTML5. kramdown-rfc2629 (Markdown for RFCs) is a backend for generating RFC XML markup from Markdown. PHP Markdown Extra adds attribute blocks, tables, and footnotes. Each registration includes contact information and references.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers eight flavors of Markdown officially, from the original to specialized versions for screenplays, RFCs, and different output formats. Each one has a name, description, and contact information for questions.

sections.title: The Variant Registry
sections.content: The RFC establishes an IANA registry for Markdown variants. Registrations are accepted on a First Come, First Served basis: anyone with a need to interoperate can register. Basic information is required: identifier, name, description, references, and contact information. Additional fields are optional and variant-specific: parameter definitions, fragment identifier syntax, and more. The registry reserves the identifiers Standard, Common, and Markdown—they cannot be registered—to prevent confusion with the generic text/markdown type. Provisional registrations can be made to reserve an identifier for three months while documentation is being prepared. This approach avoids the burden of requiring each Markdown variant to register its own media type, which would be impractical given the number of variants and their rapid evolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Communities can register their own Markdown variants with IANA so everyone knows about them. The names Standard, Common, and Markdown are reserved to avoid confusion. Anyone can start a provisional registration while they prepare documentation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Markdown as plain text is relatively harmless. Text editors need only display the text while taking care with control characters and limiting effects to the editing area. Malicious Unicode in Markdown could surreptitiously change text directionality, but a text editor should already handle this. When Markdown is processed to other formats like HTML, it inherits the security considerations of the target format. HTML can execute scripts, redirect users, download remote content, or exfiltrate personal information. Markdown may contain raw HTML islands that are passed through, transformed, or ignored depending on the processor and whether the islands are compatible. Since Markdown varies by tool and environment, a better approach is to analyze and sanitize or block the output markup rather than trying to analyze the Markdown input.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain Markdown is safe, like an email. But when Markdown is turned into HTML, it could have the same security risks as HTML: scripts that run, links that trick you, content that gets downloaded. The output should be checked, not just the input.
